name: Property-Based Testing and Fuzzing
intent: Test a rule that must hold for every input by generating many inputs from a seed, and shrink any failure to a small case you can read and replay, while knowing that the result is only as good as the generator and the property.
scenario: A run-length encoder turns "aaab" into "3a1b", with a bug: a run of 10 or more equal characters is written wrongly. Five hand-written examples pass. The team generates inputs from a seeded generator, checks that decoding an encoding returns the original, and compares three generators and a weak property.
problem: Example-based tests check the inputs their author thought of, and the bug lives in one nobody thought of. Property-based testing states a rule that must hold for all inputs, such as decode(encode(s)) equals s, and lets the machine generate many inputs to look for a counterexample. The common claim is that it finds bugs you did not imagine. The trap is that it finds only what the generator can produce and the property can detect. A uniform generator over 26 letters almost never produces a run of 10 equal letters, so it reports no failure in thousands of cases. A property such as the output is not empty can never fail. Fuzzing is the same idea with a looser property, typically that the program must not crash, fed with large volumes of mutated or generated input.

howItWorks.title: State a property, not an example
howItWorks.text: A property is a rule that holds for every valid input: decoding what you encoded gives the original, sorting twice equals sorting once, an operation is its own inverse. Finding good properties is the main skill. Round trips, invariants, comparison with a simple reference version, and idempotence are common sources.

howItWorks.title: Generate inputs from a seed
howItWorks.text: A generator builds random inputs, here strings of up to 20 characters. It is driven by a seeded random number generator, so the same seed gives the same sequence. When a case fails, the seed and the case number reproduce it exactly, which turns a random failure into a repeatable one. Print the seed on every run.

howItWorks.title: Shape the generator to find the bugs
howItWorks.text: The set of inputs that can be generated is the set of bugs that can be found. Uniform random letters rarely repeat, so long runs never appear. A small alphabet, or a generator biased toward repeating the previous character, produces runs often. Edge-heavy generators, such as empty strings, boundaries and maximum sizes, find more per case than blind randomness.

howItWorks.title: Shrink the failure
howItWorks.text: A failing input of 19 characters is hard to read. Shrinking tries smaller variants of it, such as deleting one element at a time, and keeps any that still fail, until none do. Here every failure shrinks to 10 equal characters, which shows the cause at once: the bug starts at a run of 10. Good libraries shrink automatically.

howItWorks.title: Check that the property can fail
howItWorks.text: A property that always holds proves nothing. Break the code on purpose and check that the property goes red. Run enough cases: the number that is enough depends on how rare the bug is, which you do not know in advance, so treat a pass as evidence, not as proof.

pros: Finds counterexamples nobody thought to write, especially at boundaries
A seed makes a random failure reproducible
Shrinking gives a small, locally minimal failing input that points at the cause
One property replaces dozens of near-identical example tests
cons: Good properties are hard to find, and a weak one passes forever
Results depend on the generator: what it cannot produce, it cannot test
A failure that needs a rare input may need very many cases, and runs can be slow
Generators for complex data, such as valid orders or documents, take real effort to write
whenToUse: Code with a clear rule over a wide input space: parsers, encoders, sorting, merging, serialisation
A function with an inverse, so a round trip makes a ready-made property
Hunting crashes in code that reads untrusted input, using a fuzzer
whenNotToUse: Behaviour that has no simple rule, where the property would restate the implementation
Slow tests, such as ones that call a network, where thousands of cases are unaffordable
As a replacement for a few readable examples that document the behaviour
pitfalls: Trusting 1,000 passing cases from a generator that cannot make the failing input: in the model, 26 letters never produced a run of 10
A weak property that is always true, such as the output is not empty, and a green run that means nothing
Writing the property as a copy of the implementation, so both are wrong in the same way
Not printing the seed, so a failure on CI cannot be replayed
Reading a failure's raw 19-character input and guessing, when shrinking would show the 10 characters that matter
Treating a clean fuzzing run as proof of safety, when it shows only that the inputs tried did not crash

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: States the property and reads the failure.

roles.label: Generator
roles.description: Builds inputs from a seeded random sequence.

roles.label: Encoder
roles.description: The code under test, with a hidden bug.

roles.label: Property
roles.description: The rule checked on every generated input.

roles.label: Shrinker
roles.description: Cuts a failing input down to a minimal one.

quiz.question: A property test with a uniform generator over 26 letters runs 10,000 cases without a failure, yet the encoder breaks on 10 equal letters. What is the best explanation?
options: The property is wrong, because round trips cannot find bugs.
Seeded generators are not truly random, so they skip bugs.
The code is probably correct, because 10,000 is a large number.
The generator almost never produces a run of 10 equal letters, so the bug is out of its reach.
quiz.explanation: Only inputs the generator can produce are tested. With 26 letters, 10 in a row is vanishingly rare. In the model, an a-or-b alphabet reaches the bug within 1,000 cases for each seed tried, and a generator biased toward repeats within 10.

quiz.question: A test fails on CI with a generated input, and nobody noted the seed. What is lost?
options: The ability to replay the failing case exactly, since the seed fixes the sequence of inputs.
The ability to shrink the failure, since shrinking needs the seed.
Nothing, because the property would fail the same way on any input.
The result of the property, which is stored only in the seed.
quiz.explanation: The same seed gives the same inputs in the same order, so seed plus case number reproduces a failure. Without it you must hope to hit the failure again. Shrinking works on the failing input itself.

quiz.question: What does shrinking do with a failing input of 19 characters?
options: Compresses it so it takes less space in the test report.
Replaces it with a different random input.
Tries smaller variants and keeps cutting while the input still fails, ending at a small case such as 10 equal characters.
Removes the failing property from the run.
quiz.explanation: Shrinking deletes or simplifies parts of the input while the failure remains. The shrunk case, 10 equal characters, shows what triggers the bug much more clearly than a long random string.
